title: Applied AI for Political Scientists
text:
Preface
These handouts are prepared for Applied AI for Political Scientists by Dr. Babak RezaeeDaryakenari s.rezaeedaryakenari@fsw.leidenuniv.nl.
Work through the R Bootcamp before the first session on 2 September. The Weekly Handouts accompany the sessions.
This is an ongoing project. Please do not share or use it without the author’s written permission.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 1: install R
Two separate pieces of software are needed, and the distinction between them causes more confusion than it should. R is the language: the engine that does the computing. RStudio is the environment you work in: the editor, the panes, the buttons. RStudio cannot do anything without R behind it, which is why R goes first.
Everything here is free, and the whole process takes about fifteen minutes on a normal connection. Do it before the first session on 2 September rather than during it.
Go to cran.r-project.org and choose the download link for your system.
On Windows, click Download R for Windows, then base, then the download link at the top. Run the installer and accept the defaults.
On macOS, click Download R for macOS and pick the correct .pkg file. There are usually two. If your Mac has an Apple silicon chip (M1, M2, M3, or M4), take the arm64 version. If it has an Intel chip, take the other. To check, click the Apple menu, then About This Mac, and read the Chip or Processor line.
Choosing the wrong one on a Mac is the single most common installation problem, and it produces confusing errors later rather than a clear failure at install time.

title: Four Ways to Run R Code
text:
The console: thinking out loud
Within the first hour of using RStudio you will encounter at least four different places where R code can be typed and executed: the console, a script, an R Markdown document, and a Quarto document. Students almost always assume that one of these is the real way to work and that the others are variations on it, and they then spend the semester wondering which one they were supposed to be using. The assumption is understandable, and it is wrong. The four are not competing versions of the same thing. Each answers a different question, and the question you are asking should determine which one you open.
The distinction matters more in this course than it would in an introductory statistics class. Your final project is submitted as a document that must run from raw inputs to reported numbers on a machine that is not yours. Ten percent of its grade depends on that property alone. Understanding what each of these environments preserves, and what each of them quietly discards, is therefore not a preliminary detail. It is the foundation of everything you submit.
The console is the panel where R is actually running. When you type 2 + 2 and press Enter, the console evaluates the expression, prints the answer, and forgets that you asked.
That last property is the important one. The console keeps a history you can scroll through, but it keeps no record you can hand to anyone, and it imposes no order on what you did. If you fit a model, adjust a variable, fit it again, and then produce a result you are pleased with, the console cannot tell you which sequence of steps produced it. Neither can you, a week later.
The console is therefore the right tool for questions you are asking of yourself rather than of the world. Checking the dimensions of a dataset, inspecting a variable, reading a help file, and testing whether a line does what you expect are all console work. Use it constantly, and use it freely. Nothing you do there is precious, which is precisely what makes it useful.

title: Four Ways to Run R Code
section: The script: a record of instructions
text:
The script: a record of instructions
An R script, saved with the extension .R, is a plain text file containing lines of R code and nothing else. When you run a script, R executes each line in order, exactly as if you had typed them into the console yourself.
The difference is that the file survives. A script is a record of what you did, in the order you did it, and it can be run again tomorrow, or by someone else, or by you on a different machine. This is what makes it the first genuinely reproducible unit of work, and it is why the transition from console to script is the single most consequential habit shift in learning R.
# analysis.R
library(tidyverse)

fl <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/babakrezaee/AppliedAI-PoliSci/main/data/FearonLaitin2003.csv")

fl_clean <- fl %>%
  filter(!is.na(onset)) %>%
  mutate(log_pop = log(pop))

model <- glm(onset ~ log_pop + gdpen, data = fl_clean, family = "binomial")
summary(model)
What a script preserves is the instructions. What it does not preserve is the output. Run the script and the results appear in the console, where they are as ephemeral as anything else typed there. Run it again in three months, after the data file has been updated or a package has changed, and you may get different numbers with no record of what the old ones were. Scripts are also, by design, hostile to prose. You can write comments, and you should, but a comment is a note to yourself, not an argument addressed to a reader.
Scripts remain the right choice for work whose product is an action rather than a document: downloading and cleaning a dataset, defining functions you will use elsewhere, or running a long job whose output is a saved file. In the repository for this course you will find several such scripts in the R/ folder.
crumbs: Four Ways to Run R Code

title: Four Ways to Run R Code
section: R Markdown: code, prose, and output in one file
text:
R Markdown: code, prose, and output in one file
An R Markdown document, saved as .Rmd, holds three things at once: prose written in Markdown, chunks of R code, and the output those chunks produce. When you knit the document, R runs every chunk in order, captures the results, and weaves them into a finished report as HTML, PDF, or Word.
---
title: "Civil War Onset"
output: html_document
---

Fearon and Laitin (2003) report that per capita income predicts
civil war onset more reliably than measures of ethnic diversity.
The model below reproduces that pattern.

```{r}
model <- glm(onset ~ gdpen + ethfrac, data = fl, family = "binomial")
summary(model)
```

The coefficient on income is negative and precisely estimated,
while the coefficient on ethnic fractionalization is not
distinguishable from zero.
Two consequences follow, and both matter for this course.
The first is that the numbers in your text cannot drift away from the numbers your code produced, because the document generates them each time it is knitted. A reported coefficient that was copied by hand into a sentence will eventually become wrong, quietly, when the analysis changes and the sentence does not. A reported coefficient that is produced by the code cannot.
The second is subtler and catches almost everyone at least once. Knitting starts a fresh R session that knows nothing about your workspace. Any object you created in the console, any package you loaded by hand, and any file path that happens to work on your machine are all invisible to it. A document that runs perfectly line by line in your own session will therefore fail to knit if it depends on something you did outside it. This is not an inconvenience to be worked around. It is the mechanism that makes the format trustworthy, because a document that knits from a clean session is a document that will run on someone else’s computer.
The habit that follows is simple and worth adopting now: before you submit anything, restart R (Session, then Restart R) and knit. If it does not run from clean, it does not run.
crumbs: Four Ways to Run R Code

title: Four Ways to Run R Code
section: Quarto: the same idea, more broadly
text:
Quarto: the same idea, more broadly
Quarto, saved as .qmd, is the successor to R Markdown. Everything described above applies to it unchanged, and if you have understood R Markdown you already understand Quarto.
The differences are largely a matter of reach. Quarto is not tied to R, so the same document can execute chunks written in Python or Julia, which is directly relevant given that most of the applied AI ecosystem lives in Python. Its options are declared in a consistent way across output formats, and it renders books and websites as readily as single documents. The materials you are reading now are a Quarto book.
```{r}
#| label: fig-onset
#| fig-cap: "Predicted probability of onset by income"
#| warning: false

ggplot(fl, aes(x = gdpen, y = fitted)) +
  geom_line()
```
For a single analysis document the practical difference between the two is small, and either is acceptable for your final project. I use Quarto for course materials because it handles a multi-chapter book cleanly, and I would suggest it for new work on the general principle that development effort is going there rather than into R Markdown.
crumbs: Four Ways to Run R Code

The rule of thumb is short. Explore in the console, because it costs nothing and you will throw the work away. Automate in a script, when the product is an action rather than an argument. Report in Quarto or R Markdown, when someone else needs to see both what you concluded and how you got there.
Your final project falls squarely in the third category, which is why the submission format is a .qmd or .Rmd file together with the document it renders. The requirement is not a formatting preference. A project submitted as a script and a separate write-up cannot demonstrate that the numbers in the write-up came from the script, and demonstrating exactly that is a substantial part of what the project is for.

title: Four Ways to Run R Code
text:
Exercise
Work through this in order. It takes about fifteen minutes and it is worth doing before the first session rather than during it.

In the console, compute mean(c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)). Note that the answer appears and then nothing remains except a history entry.
Open a new script (File, New File, R Script). Write the same line, save the file as first-script.R, and run it with the Source button. The result appears in the console again, but the instruction now lives in a file you could send to someone.
Open a new Quarto document (File, New File, Quarto Document). Write one sentence of prose describing what you are about to compute, then a code chunk containing the same line, then one sentence interpreting the result. Render it.
Now break it deliberately. In the console, create an object with x <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42). Change the chunk in your Quarto document to mean(x) and render again.

The render fails, and the error will say that x was not found. Sit with that for a moment before fixing it, because you have just met the most common reason a working analysis refuses to knit the night before a deadline. The object exists in your session and does not exist in the document. The fix is to define x inside the document, which is also the reason the format can be trusted.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Assignment
Everything in R is an object, and almost everything you will do in this course amounts to creating an object, inspecting it, and passing it to a function. This chapter covers the three kinds of object you will meet constantly: the vector, which holds a column of values; the data frame, which holds a table of them; and the individual value, which is really just a vector of length one.
The order matters. Data frames are what political science data actually look like, and they are the destination. Vectors come first because a data frame is built out of them, and because most of the errors you will hit in Week 2 come from a vector quietly being the wrong type.
An object is created by assigning something a name. R accepts two operators for this, and you will see both in the wild.
Use <-. The two are equivalent in this context, but = also means other things in R, including naming an argument inside a function call, so keeping the two visually distinct saves confusion later. In RStudio, Alt and minus on Windows or Option and minus on a Mac types it for you.
To see what an object contains, type its name.
To remove one, use rm().
Names are subject to a few rules. They may contain letters, numbers, a period, and an underscore, but not spaces or symbols such as !, +, or #. They cannot begin with a number. And R is case sensitive, so polity and Polity are two different objects, which is a more common source of “object not found” than anyone expects.

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
The problem, stated plainly
Code that runs on your machine and code that runs are not the same thing. The gap between them is where most of the marks on your final project’s reproducibility criterion are lost, and almost all of it comes down to a handful of habits that cost nothing once you have them.
This chapter is about those habits. None of the material is difficult. What makes it worth a chapter is that the failures it prevents do not appear until the moment they are most expensive, which is when someone else opens your work.
Suppose you write this at the top of an analysis.
On your laptop, in that folder, it works. Everywhere else it fails, because no other computer has that folder. Your instructor does not have it, your co-author or colleague does not have it, and neither will you after you reorganize your files in March.
setwd() is the most common single reason a submitted document does not run. You will see it constantly in older code, including in tutorials and in published replication files, and the instinct to copy it is understandable. Do not. Nothing in this course requires it, and using it may cost you points on the project.
The replacement is not a different function. It is a different way of organizing work.

title: Reading Data into R
text:
CSV, the ordinary case
Importing data feels like the trivial step before the real work, and it is where a surprising share of analytical errors are born. The reason is that R almost never refuses to import a file. It makes a decision about what your data mean, tells you nothing, and carries on. A column of numbers arrives as text, a missing value code of -99 is treated as a real observation, and everything downstream is quietly wrong.
This chapter covers the formats you will actually meet and, more importantly, the check that catches the failures.
A comma-separated (CSV) file is plain text with one row per line and commas between fields. It is the format most political science data arrive in, and R reads it out of the box.
There is also a tidyverse version, read_csv(), with an underscore rather than a period.
Three differences matter in practice. read_csv() is faster on large files, it prints a summary of the column types it guessed, which is useful information rather than clutter, and it returns a tibble rather than a data frame. A tibble is a data frame with better printing behavior, and everything you learned in the previous chapter applies to it unchanged.
Either is acceptable in this course. The handouts use read.csv() because it needs no package, so the first line of a chapter always runs.

title: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI
text:
What kind of question are we asking?
Week 1, 2 September
This first session has two purposes. First, we need to distinguish between correlation, causation, prediction, and forecasting. These are related, but they are not the same research goal, and confusing them can produce bad research. Second, we need a working vocabulary for talking about artificial intelligence. Terms such as machine learning, generative AI, reasoning model, and agent are often used as though they refer to the same thing. They do not.
There is no code in this handout. The work this week is conceptual. That may sound less exciting than fitting a model, but it matters. A model can be technically impressive and still answer the wrong question. The same problem appears in public debates about AI, where a loose use of one term can hide who designed a system, what it actually does, and who is responsible when it fails.
Developing a theoretical argument about a political phenomenon is work you do across the programme. This course adds three things to it. We ask how evidence can be used to evaluate an argument. We ask how statistical and machine-learning models can be used to anticipate outcomes. And we treat AI systems themselves as objects of political analysis, because they are increasingly part of how states, parties, platforms, and administrations act.
Political scientists use qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-method research designs. All three can be empirical, and they share an underlying scientific principle: theoretical claims should be exposed to evidence that could count against them.
For Popper, a theory is scientific when it produces claims that are empirically testable and open to falsification. This does not mean that one study can prove a theory. Evidence can support a hypothesis without proving that it is true. That support remains provisional and depends on the quality of the research design, the measurement, and the alternatives that have been considered.
Lakatos asks us to look beyond the fate of one hypothesis and consider the development of a research programme (Lakatos 1970). Does it generate new expectations and improve our understanding, or does it survive only because its supporters keep adding qualifications after every failure? We will return to this question when we compare models: improving performance is useful, but adding complexity without learning anything substantive is not necessarily scientific progress.
The same care is needed when discussing null hypotheses. Rejecting a null hypothesis can provide support for a substantive alternative. Failing to reject a null hypothesis is also evidence from the study and can be informative, particularly when the design is strong and the test has adequate power. It does not prove the null hypothesis. More generally, when observations remain consistent with the implications of a theory, we may describe this as empirical support, not as final confirmation.
Publishing research is therefore an invitation to other scholars to attack the argument scientifically: to examine the assumptions, repeat the analysis, use other data, and try to show that the finding does not hold.
The four questions below organize the first part of the course.
Forecasting is a form of prediction in a technical sense, but we keep it as a separate category in this course. The temporal dimension creates additional problems that deserve separate attention.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Vectors
A vector is an ordered collection of values of the same type. You build one with c(), for combine.
gdp <- c(2.1, 4.7, 1.3, 8.9)
gdp
#> [1] 2.1 4.7 1.3 8.9
Sequences of consecutive integers have a shorthand.
years <- 1990:1995
years
#> [1] 1990 1991 1992 1993 1994 1995
The phrase “of the same type” is the part worth pausing on, and it is where the first real surprise lives.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Types, and why they matter
A vector holds numbers, or text, or logical values, but never a mixture. If you supply a mixture, R does not complain. It silently converts everything to the most accommodating type, which is almost always text.
v1 <- c(1, 2, 3)
v2 <- c(1, 2, "a")

v1
#> [1] 1 2 3

v2
#> [1] "1" "2" "a"
Look closely at v2. The numbers now have quotation marks around them. They are no longer numbers, and arithmetic on them will fail.
mean(v2)
#> Warning: argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA
This behavior, called coercion, is the single most common reason a calculation returns NA for no visible reason. A real dataset with one stray text entry in an otherwise numeric column, for instance a "n/a" typed by hand, will import as a text column and every subsequent calculation on it will quietly fail.
The habit that protects you is to check the type whenever a result surprises you.
class(v1)
#> [1] "numeric"

class(v2)
#> [1] "character"
Logical vectors hold TRUE and FALSE, and you will meet them constantly as the result of a comparison.
gdp > 3
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Arithmetic happens element by element
Operations on vectors apply to every element at once, which is why R rarely needs the loops that other languages depend on.
a <- c(1, 3, 5, 7)
b <- c(1, 2, 4, 8)

a * 5
#> [1]  5 15 25 35

a + b
#> [1]  2  5  9 15
If the two vectors are of unequal length, R recycles the shorter one to match the longer, rather than raising an error.
c(10, 20) + c(1, 2, 3, 4)
#> [1] 11 22 13 24
This is occasionally convenient and frequently dangerous. If you did not intend the recycling, you now have a result that looks plausible and is wrong. When two vectors should be the same length, check with length() before combining them.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
section: Getting at parts of a vector
text:
Getting at parts of a vector
Square brackets extract elements by position, counting from one rather than from zero.
gdp[2]
#> [1] 4.7

gdp[c(1, 3)]
#> [1] 2.1 1.3

gdp[-1]        # everything except the first
#> [1] 4.7 1.3 8.9
You can also select with a logical condition, which is the form you will use most.
gdp[gdp > 3]
#> [1] 4.7 8.9

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Missing values
Missing data is written NA, and it is contagious by design.
pop <- c(12, 45, NA, 8)
mean(pop)
#> [1] NA
R is telling you something true: the mean of a set that includes an unknown value is unknown. If you are content to ignore the missing case, say so explicitly.
mean(pop, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 21.66667
Say so deliberately rather than reflexively. Dropping missing cases is a substantive decision about your sample, and the final project asks you to make such decisions visible rather than silent.
To find them:
is.na(pop)
#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

sum(is.na(pop))
#> [1] 1

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Data frames
A data frame is a table: several vectors of equal length standing side by side as columns, each with a name, each with its own type. This is what a political science dataset is.
Load one. The read.csv() function accepts a web address directly, so nothing needs downloading.
fl <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/babakrezaee/AppliedAI-PoliSci/main/data/FearonLaitin2003.csv")
These are the data behind Fearon and Laitin’s 2003 article on ethnicity, insurgency, and civil war, one of the most cited studies in the conflict literature. The unit of analysis is the country-year, and we will return to it in Week 6.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Look before you calculate
Before doing anything with a new dataset, find out what you have.
dim(fl)          # rows and columns
nrow(fl)
names(fl)        # column names
head(fl, n = 3)  # first three rows
str(fl)          # structure: every column, its type, first few values
str() is the most useful of these, because it reports the type of every column. A numeric variable that arrived as text will announce itself here rather than three steps later.
For a single variable, summary() gives the distribution and, importantly, the count of missing values.
summary(fl$gdpen)
The dollar sign extracts one column by name. It is the workhorse of base R and you will use it constantly.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
section: An example of why you look first
text:
An example of why you look first
The outcome variable in these data is onset, coded one in a country-year when a civil war begins and zero otherwise. Count its values.
table(fl$onset)
You will find a handful of zeros and ones, as expected, and also a single observation coded 4. That is a data entry error, present in the distributed file, and it has survived into a great many replications.
It matters. A model fitted with onset treated as numeric would take that four seriously. Left as a factor with three levels, a classifier would try to predict a category that occurs once in six thousand cases. Either way the result is wrong in a manner no error message will announce.
The fix is one line.
fl$onset[fl$onset > 1] <- 1
table(fl$onset)
The lesson generalizes beyond this dataset. Run table() on every categorical variable and summary() on every numeric one before you model anything. It takes two minutes and it is the cheapest error-catching you will ever do.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Selecting rows and columns
Data frames take two indices inside the brackets, rows first and columns second.
fl[1, ]            # first row, all columns
fl[, "onset"]      # the onset column
fl[1:5, c("country", "year", "onset")]
To keep rows meeting a condition:
africa <- fl[fl$ssafrica == 1, ]
nrow(africa)
Note the double equals sign. A single = assigns; a double == asks whether two things are equal. Mixing them up is a rite of passage.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
The tidyverse, and the pipe
Base R can do everything above, and for many tasks the tidyverse offers a version that reads more like a sentence. Install it once, then load it in each session.
# install.packages("tidyverse")   # once, ever
library(tidyverse)                # every session
The pipe operator %>% takes whatever is on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on its right. Written this way, a chain of operations reads in the order it happens.
fl %>%
  filter(ssafrica == 1, year >= 1980) %>%
  select(country, year, onset, gdpen) %>%
  head()
Compare that with the base R equivalent, which has to be read from the inside out:
head(fl[fl$ssafrica == 1 & fl$year >= 1980, c("country", "year", "onset", "gdpen")])
Both are correct. The piped version is easier to modify six weeks later, which is why the handouts use it. In RStudio, Cmd and Shift and M on a Mac, or Ctrl and Shift and M on Windows, types the pipe.
Three verbs will carry most of your work. filter() keeps rows, select() keeps columns, and mutate() creates new ones.
fl %>%
  filter(!is.na(gdpen)) %>%
  mutate(log_pop = log(pop)) %>%
  select(country, year, gdpen, log_pop) %>%
  head()

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Factors
A factor is R’s type for a categorical variable: values drawn from a fixed set of levels. Modeling functions expect categorical outcomes as factors, so you will convert deliberately.
fl$onset <- factor(fl$onset)
levels(fl$onset)
#> [1] "0" "1"
One warning worth carrying. Converting a factor straight to numeric returns the level codes, not the labels, so a factor with levels “0” and “1” becomes 1 and 2. If you need the underlying numbers, route through character first.
as.numeric(as.character(fl$onset))

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Matrices, briefly
A matrix is a rectangle of values that are all the same type, which is the difference from a data frame. You will not build many, but they appear inside modeling functions, and older code uses cbind() and rbind() to assemble them.
m <- matrix(c(2, 4, 3, 1, 5, 7), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
m
t(m)               # transpose
cbind(m, c(7, 4, 2))  # add a column
Recognizing them is enough for now. Week 4 returns to matrices when text becomes a document-term matrix.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Getting help
Every function has a help page, reachable with a question mark.
?mean
?read.csv
The Examples section at the bottom is usually the fastest way in, because you can run those lines directly. If you do not know the function’s name, ??regression searches the text of all installed help pages.

title: Objects, Vectors, and Data Frames
text:
Exercise
Roughly twenty minutes. Do it in a script rather than the console, so you still have it afterward.

Create a numeric vector of five values and a character vector of five country names. Confirm the type of each with class().
Combine one number and one country name into a single vector with c(). Check its class. Explain in a comment what happened and why.
Load the Fearon and Laitin data. Report how many rows and columns it has.
Run table() on onset. Note the anomaly, correct it, and run table() again to confirm.
Using the pipe, keep only country-years from 1990 onward with onset equal to one, and select country, year, and gdpen. How many civil war onsets does that leave?
Compute the mean of gdpen across the whole dataset. It returns NA. Work out why, then compute it in a way that succeeds, and add a comment saying what your version is actually the mean of.

Step 6 is the one that matters. Every dataset you meet in this course has missing values, and the difference between a mean of the observed cases and a mean of the sample is a difference you will have to state plainly in your final project.

read.csv("civil_war.csv")

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
R Projects
An R Project is a folder that R treats as the home of a piece of work. Creating one puts a small file with the extension .Rproj inside the folder, and from then on, opening that file does three useful things at once: it starts a fresh R session, it sets the working directory to that folder, and it remembers which files you had open.
That second point is the whole trick. Because the working directory is already correct, you never have to set it, and because it is set relative to the project rather than to your machine, the same code works on anyone else’s computer.
To create one: File > New Project > New Directory > New Project, then give the folder a name and a location. For work you already have in a folder, use File > New Project > Existing Directory instead.
From then on, open the project by double-clicking the .Rproj file rather than by opening a script directly. If you open a .qmd from the Finder, R starts with no project and the paths will not resolve, which produces a “cannot open file” error that looks like a problem with the file and is not.

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
Relative paths
Inside a project, you refer to files by their location relative to the project folder, with no leading slash and no drive letter.
dat <- read.csv("data/civil_war.csv")
That line means “the file civil_war.csv, inside a folder called data, inside whatever folder this project lives in.” It is true on every machine.
A few conventions worth following:

Forward slashes, /, on every operating system, including Windows. R accepts them everywhere.
No spaces in file or folder names. Use civil_war.csv rather than civil war.csv. Spaces are legal, but they will eventually bite you.
Lower case, consistently. Some systems treat Data/ and data/ as the same folder and some do not.

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
A layout that works
You do not need an elaborate structure. This is enough for the final project and it will still make sense a year from now.
YourProject/
  YourProject.Rproj
  analysis.qmd          the document you submit
  data/
    raw/                exactly as downloaded, never edited
    processed/          anything your code produced
  R/
    clean-data.R        scripts that do a job
  figures/              plots your code saved
The distinction between data/raw/ and data/processed/ is the one that earns its keep. Raw files are never opened in Excel and never edited by hand. Every change is made in code, which means every change is visible, reversible, and explicable when a reviewer, instructor, or colleague asks why your sample has 4,318 rows rather than 4,502.

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
Note on this course
The handouts here load their data straight from a web address, so there are no local files to find.
fl <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/babakrezaee/AppliedAI-PoliSci/main/data/FearonLaitin2003.csv")
That is deliberate. It means the code in every chapter runs for you immediately, on any machine, with nothing downloaded.
Your final project is different. You will have data files of your own, and the paths in your document will have to resolve on a machine that is not yours. The habits in this chapter are for that, and it is suggested to adopted for your final project.

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
Never save the workspace
By default, R offers to save your objects when you quit and to reload them when you return. Turn this off.
Tools > Global Options > General, then set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never, and untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup.
The reason is that a restored workspace hides broken code. An object created three weeks ago by a line you have since deleted is still sitting in memory, so your analysis appears to work while depending on something that no longer exists anywhere in your files. The failure surfaces when you knit, or when someone else runs it, which is exactly the wrong time.
Your objects should always be recreatable by running your code. If they are not, the code is incomplete.

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
Restart, and run from clean
The companion habit is to restart R often. Session > Restart R, or Cmd and Shift and F10 on a Mac, Ctrl and Shift and F10 on Windows.
After restarting, run your document from the top. If it completes, it works. If it does not, you have found a dependency on something that existed only in your session, and you have found it now rather than the night before a deadline.
Do this before every submission, without exception. It is the entire test, and it takes under a minute.

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
Packages
Load every package you use at the top of the document, in one place.
library(tidyverse)
library(caret)
Do not put install.packages() in a document you submit. Installation is something you do once on your own machine, from the console. Left in a document, it re-installs packages on the reader’s computer, which is slow, occasionally destructive, and never what they wanted.
If a package is missing, the reader gets a clear error naming it, which is the correct outcome. A short note in your README saying which packages the project needs is a courtesy worth extending.

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
Seeds
Anything involving randomness, which in this course means splitting data into training and test sets, sampling, and fitting a random forest, gives a different answer each time it runs.
set.seed(7)
Put that line near the top, once, before anything random happens. The number itself is arbitrary and does not matter. What matters is that with it, your reported numbers reproduce exactly, and without it, a reader who runs your code gets results that disagree with your text for no stated reason.

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
When a path fails anyway
The error will look like this.
Warning: cannot open file 'data/civil_war.csv': No such file or directory
Error in file(file, "rt") : cannot open the connection
Three checks, in order.
Where does R think it is?
getwd()
If that is not your project folder, you opened the file without opening the project. Close everything and open the .Rproj file.
Does R see the file?
list.files("data")
If the file is not listed, the problem is the name or the location, not the code.
Is the name exactly right? Capital letters count. So does the extension, and macOS hides extensions by default, so a file that looks like civil_war.csv in the Finder may actually be civil_war.csv.txt.
Notice that the fix is never setwd().

title: Projects, Paths, and Reproducible Habits
text:
Exercise
About fifteen minutes.

Create a new R Project called ai-practice, somewhere you will find it again.
Inside the project folder, create a data folder. In the RStudio Files pane, use the New Folder button.
Download the Fearon and Laitin file into it, using code rather than your browser:
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/babakrezaee/AppliedAI-PoliSci/main/data/FearonLaitin2003.csv",
  destfile = "data/FearonLaitin2003.csv"
)
Write a script that loads it with a relative path and reports its dimensions. Save the script as explore.R.
Set the workspace options as described above. Then restart R and run your script from the top. It should work with an empty environment.
Now break it on purpose. Change the path to Data/FearonLaitin2003.csv, with a capital D, and run it again. Read the error carefully, then run getwd() and list.files("data") and confirm what each one tells you.

Step 6 is the useful one. That error message will find you again during the block, and recognizing it in ten seconds rather than twenty minutes is the only thing separating an evening’s work from an evening’s frustration.

title: Reading Data into R
text:
fl <- read.csv("data/FearonLaitin2003.csv")

library(tidyverse)
fl <- read_csv("data/FearonLaitin2003.csv")

title: Reading Data into R
text:
Straight from a web address
Both functions accept a URL wherever they accept a filename, which means data can be loaded with nothing downloaded.
fl <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/babakrezaee/AppliedAI-PoliSci/main/data/FearonLaitin2003.csv")
This is how every dataset in these handouts is loaded. It has two advantages worth naming: the code runs identically on any machine, and there is no file path to get wrong.
It has one disadvantage. If the address ever changes, the code stops working, and if the file behind the address is edited, your results change without your knowing. For the final project, download the file once and put it on your cloud-based platform, then you have control over your data source than relying on someone else’s server.
Note the address on Github must be the raw one. Clicking a CSV on GitHub shows a formatted preview page, and its address returns HTML rather than data. The Raw button gives the address you want, and it always begins raw.githubusercontent.com. You can also upload your files on Dropbox, Googledrive, and Onedrive; just make sure that you have the permission to put the files on these public cloud-based platforms.

title: Reading Data into R
text:
Check the import, every time
This is the habit the chapter exists for. Three lines, immediately after loading anything.
dim(fl)
str(fl)
summary(fl)
You are looking for three things.
Did every column get the type you expected? A numeric variable listed as chr in the str() output has a non-numeric value hiding in it somewhere.
Are the row and column counts right? If the file should have 6,610 rows and you have 6,609, the header row was probably read as data, or the last line lacks a line break.
Do the ranges make sense? summary() reports the minimum and maximum of each numeric column. A polity2 score of -88 or a population of -99 is a missing value code, not an observation, and it will wreck any model that takes it seriously.

title: Reading Data into R
text:
Missing value codes
Older datasets frequently encode missing values as numbers, with -99, -999, and -88 being the common choices. R has no way of knowing this and will treat them as real.
Tell it explicitly at import.
dat <- read.csv("data/survey.csv", na.strings = c("NA", "", "-99", "-999"))
Or fix it afterward, which is clearer when only some columns are affected.
dat$income[dat$income == -99] <- NA
Either way, do it before anything else. A mean computed over a column containing -99 is not slightly wrong, it is meaningless, and nothing in the output will tell you.

title: Reading Data into R
section: When the commas are not commas
text:
When the commas are not commas
Files exported from Excel on a European system are often separated by semicolons rather than commas, and they use commas as decimal points. Opening one with read.csv() produces a single column of text.
dat <- read.csv2("data/dutch_export.csv")   # semicolons, comma decimals
dat <- read_csv2("data/dutch_export.csv")   # tidyverse equivalent
Worth knowing here rather than elsewhere, since Dutch-locale Excel does this by default and several of you will hit it with data you export yourselves.
If the separator is something else entirely, such as a tab, say so:
dat <- read.delim("data/file.txt")                    # tab separated
dat <- read.csv("data/file.txt", sep = "|")           # anything else
The fastest way to diagnose any of this is to open the file in a plain text editor and look at the first two lines. Two minutes of looking beats an hour of guessing.

title: Reading Data into R
text:
Accented characters
Country names, party names, and any text data will contain characters outside plain English. If they arrive mangled, as Ã© where é belongs, the file’s encoding was misread.
dat <- read.csv("data/parties.csv", encoding = "UTF-8")
UTF-8 is correct for the large majority of files you will meet. This will matter in Week 4, when text becomes data.

title: Reading Data into R
text:
Excel files
Excel files are not text and cannot be read by read.csv(). Use readxl.
# install.packages("readxl")
library(readxl)

dat <- read_excel("data/data.xlsx")
dat <- read_excel("data/data.xlsx", sheet = "Coding")   # a named sheet
dat <- read_excel("data/data.xlsx", skip = 3)           # skip title rows
skip earns its place. Spreadsheets kept by humans very often carry a title, a blank line, and a note before the actual header row, and without skip all of that is read as data.
A note on Excel more generally. It is a reasonable place to receive data and a poor place to edit it, because changes made by hand leave no record. If a value must change, change it in R, where the change is visible in your code and reversible.

title: Reading Data into R
text:
Stata and SPSS
Political science data arrive as .dta and .sav more often than anyone would like. The haven package reads both.
# install.packages("haven")
library(haven)

dat <- read_dta("data/anes.dta")   # Stata
dat <- read_sav("data/ess.sav")    # SPSS
Older tutorials recommend foreign and Hmisc for this. Both still work, and haven handles recent file versions and preserves variable labels better, so prefer it.
Labelled columns from these formats sometimes behave unexpectedly in models. If one gives you trouble, strip the labels:
dat$party <- haven::zap_labels(dat$party)

title: Reading Data into R
text:
Saving
To hand data to someone who may not use R, write a CSV.
write.csv(dat, "data/processed/cleaned.csv", row.names = FALSE)
row.names = FALSE matters. Without it, R adds a column of row numbers, and a file that is written and read a few times accumulates several of them.
To save an R object for your own later use, including model objects and anything else a CSV cannot hold, use saveRDS().
saveRDS(model, "output/model.rds")
model <- readRDS("output/model.rds")
This is worth knowing for the final project, or algorithms that take a longer time to run, such as Random Forest. A model that takes several minutes to fit can be fitted once, saved, and read back, so that re-rendering the document does not refit it.

title: Reading Data into R
text:
Exercise
About twenty minutes. Work in the ai-practice project from the previous chapter.

Load the Fearon and Laitin data from the raw URL and confirm its dimensions.
Run str() on it. List two columns that arrived as text. For each, say whether that is correct or whether it should have been numeric.
Run summary(fl$polity2). Look at the minimum. Polity scores are defined on a range of minus ten to plus ten. Is anything outside it, and if so, what do you think those values mean?
Make a deliberately awkward file. In the console:
messy <- data.frame(
  country = c("França", "Türkiye", "España"),
  score   = c(1.5, -99, 3.2)
)
write.csv(messy, "data/messy.csv", row.names = FALSE)
Read it back with read.csv("data/messy.csv"), then compute mean(score). Now read it again treating -99 as missing, and compute the mean a second time. Report both numbers and say which one you would put in a paper.
Check whether the accented characters survived the round trip. If they did not, read the file again with encoding = "UTF-8".

Step 4 is the point. Two defensible-looking numbers come out of the same file, and only one of them means anything. Nothing in R’s output distinguishes them for you.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 2: install RStudio
Go to posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop. The page detects your system and offers the right installer. Take the free Desktop version; there is no need for any paid tier or for RStudio Server.
Install it, then open RStudio, not R. From here on, RStudio is the only one of the two you will launch directly.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 3: check that it worked
You should see four panes, or two panes with tabs. Find the Console, on the left, and type this at the > prompt, then press Enter.
2 + 2
If [1] 4 appears, both pieces are installed and talking to each other.
Then check the version:
R.version.string
Anything from R 4.3.0 onward is fine for this course. If you have an older installation lying around from a previous course, update it now rather than debugging a version problem in Week 3.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 4: install the packages
A package is a bundle of functions someone else has written and shared. R ships with a great many built in, and everything else is installed once and then loaded whenever needed.
Run this in the Console. It will take several minutes and produce a large amount of scrolling output, which is normal.
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "rmarkdown", "knitr"))
Then confirm they load:
library(tidyverse)
You will see a short message listing the packages that came along with it and noting a couple of conflicts. That message is informational, not an error.
The remaining packages, for classification, text, and language model work, are installed in the week they are first needed. There is no advantage to installing everything now.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
Step 5: install Quarto
Quarto renders documents that combine code, prose, and output, and your final project is submitted in that form.
Recent versions of RStudio include it already. Check in the Console:
quarto::quarto_version()
If that returns a version number, you are done. If it reports that the package is not installed, run install.packages("quarto") and try again. If it still cannot find Quarto itself, download it from quarto.org/docs/get-started and install it separately.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
When installation goes wrong
Three problems account for nearly all of them.
“Package not available” or a compilation error on macOS. Almost always the arm64 and Intel mismatch from Step 1. Uninstall R, check your chip, and install the matching version.
Permission denied, or the installation appears to succeed but the package will not load. Common on university-managed laptops, where the default library folder is not writable. R usually offers to use a personal library instead, and you should accept. If it does not offer, run this once and then reinstall:
dir.create(Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER"), recursive = TRUE)
The download stalls or times out. More often a network problem than a problem with your machine. Try again, and if it persists, try a different connection or a different CRAN mirror, which you can choose under Tools > Global Options > Packages.
If none of these apply, bring the laptop to the first session. A five-minute look in person is faster than an evening of email, and installation problems are common enough that nobody should feel behind because of one.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
A little configuration
Two settings are worth changing now. Go to Tools > Global Options > General and:

Set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never.
Untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup.

Chapter 3 explains why these matter. In short, they are what make it possible to trust that your code actually works rather than merely appearing to.
While you are in Global Options, Appearance lets you change the theme and font size. Not important, but you will be looking at this window for eight weeks, so it is worth a minute.

title: Installing R and RStudio
text:
Before you move on
You should be able to open RStudio, type 2 + 2 in the Console, get 4, and run library(tidyverse) without an error.
That is the whole requirement. The next chapter starts from there.

title: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI
text:
Correlation
Sometimes our research is descriptive. We want to know whether two variables are associated and how strong that association is. Descriptive and correlational research has sometimes been downplayed following the causal-inference revolution in economics and political science. That is unfortunate. Description is often the first step in bringing a new political phenomenon into view, and a reliable pattern can be important even before its cause is established.
Consider the long-standing debate about economic development and democracy. There is a well-known association between them: wealthier countries tend, on average, to be more democratic. But that association does not tell us which way the causal arrow runs. Economic development may encourage democratization. Democracy may contribute to economic development. A third factor may affect both, or the relationship may run in both directions.
We can present the distinction schematically:
Correlation
\[Economic~development \overset{?; +/-}{\longleftrightarrow} Political~development\]
Possible causal relationships
\[Economic~development \overset{+/-}{\longrightarrow} Political~development\]
\[Economic~development \overset{+/-}{\longleftarrow} Political~development\]
The correlation is a finding. The arrows are additional claims that require additional evidence.
crumbs: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI

title: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI
text:
Causation
A causal study needs an identification strategy: an argument about why the estimated relationship can be interpreted as the effect of \(X\) on \(Y\), rather than as selection, reverse causation, measurement error, or the influence of an omitted factor. Calling \(X\) an independent variable does not automatically make it exogenous. Exogeneity is an assumption that must be defended through the design.
Bias is also worth defining carefully. In statistical terms, an estimator is biased when its expected value differs systematically from the parameter it is intended to estimate. This is not the same as finding that one estimate is statistically significant. Omitted variables, selection, and measurement problems are among the reasons an estimate may fail to recover the causal quantity we care about.

The experimental ideal
Randomized experiments provide a particularly clear identification strategy. In one of my research projects, I examined whether information about the principles of nonviolent resistance changes attitudes toward this form of political action. Participants were randomly assigned to two groups. One group watched a clip about International Relations. The other watched a clip about nonviolent resistance. I then compared their average attitudes after the intervention.
Random assignment means that treatment status is independent of participants’ pre-treatment characteristics by design. Across repeated random assignments, the groups are comparable on average. In one realized experiment, however, the groups do not have to be perfectly identical on every characteristic. Covariate summaries can help us describe the sample and identify surprising imbalances, but they do not make the assignment random; the assignment procedure does that.
The comparison between the two groups gives us an estimate of the average effect of receiving the information in that study. Notice how much work the design is doing. The difference in outcomes becomes interpretable because the intervention was assigned, rather than selected by participants.


Observational data
Political scientists often cannot conduct experiments. Think about conflict research. Can we randomly assign some countries to civil war and others to peace in order to study the economic consequences? Of course not.
We therefore rely on observational data produced by political and social processes that we do not control. If we want to estimate the effect of democracy on economic development, countries are not assigned randomly to different levels of democracy. Democratic countries may also have stronger state institutions, more secure property rights, different colonial histories, or other characteristics that affect economic performance.
Adding observed confounders to a model may reduce some of these problems, but it does not automatically solve them. Matching, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, panel designs, and other methods can support an identification strategy under particular assumptions. Developing those strategies is outside the scope of this course. Recognizing when a claim requires one is not.
crumbs: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI

title: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI
text:
Prediction
Prediction changes the question. Given what we know about a case, how accurately can we estimate its outcome?
Suppose we want to predict civil-war onset. Income, terrain, state capacity, political institutions, conflict history, and regional conditions may all carry useful information. A predictive model combines that information and is evaluated by how well it performs on cases it did not use for fitting.
This is different from estimating the causal effect of one variable. A model may predict well even when some of its inputs are only proxies. Imagine a bank using postal code to predict loan default. Postal code may carry information about income, employment, housing, and ethnicity. It can therefore be useful for prediction without providing a causal explanation of why a person defaults. Intervening on the postal code would not necessarily change the outcome.
Shmueli distinguishes explanatory modeling from predictive modeling (Shmueli 2010). Cranmer and Desmarais argue that political science has paid too little attention to predictive performance (Cranmer and Desmarais 2017). Hofman, Sharma, and Watts make a related case for taking prediction more seriously when evaluating explanations of social phenomena (Hofman et al. 2017). None of this means that accuracy should replace theory or causal identification.
Predictive performance can discipline an explanation. If an account repeatedly fails to anticipate the phenomenon it claims to explain, we have reason to examine it more closely. But predictive performance is not the same thing as causal evidence, and strong prediction is not sufficient for a good explanation. Social outcomes can also contain substantial noise, which means that a credible causal explanation will not always generate highly accurate individual predictions.
The purpose of the model therefore matters. If the task is prediction, performance on unseen cases is central. Flexible functional forms may be useful even when no single coefficient provides a simple substantive interpretation. If the task is causal inference, good test-set accuracy does not rescue a weak identification strategy.
crumbs: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI

title: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI
text:
Forecasting
Forecasting asks about outcomes that have not happened yet.
Suppose we have housing-price data from 1990 to 2026. We fit a model using observations from 1990 to 2019 and test it on sales from 2020 to 2026. When the model estimates the price of a house sold in 2023, it is making a prediction for a case whose outcome was hidden from the model but is already known to us. We can calculate the error immediately.
If we use the same model to estimate prices in 2027 or 2028, we are forecasting. The outcomes do not yet exist, so the forecast cannot be fully evaluated until time passes.
When forecasting is the goal, we normally divide training and test data by time rather than at random. A random split could allow a model trained on 2025 observations to predict an outcome from 2010. That may be acceptable for some prediction tasks, but it does not simulate the information problem faced by someone trying to anticipate the future.
A temporal test set is still not a genuine forecast. It is a simulation of forecasting using outcomes that are already known to the researcher. It tells us how the model would have performed in a previous period. It cannot guarantee that relationships will remain stable when the model is used later. Early-warning systems such as ViEWS (Hegre et al. 2019) produce forecasts in real time and can be fully judged only after the forecast period has passed.
crumbs: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI

title: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI
text:
Supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised learning
Supervised learning uses labeled examples. If country-years in the training data are labeled as war or peace, or parliamentary motions are labeled by topic, the model learns a mapping from the features to those known labels. The classifiers in Weeks 2 through 4 are supervised-learning methods.
Unsupervised learning starts without an outcome label. It looks for structure in the data, such as clusters of similar cases or dimensions along which cases vary. Because there is no known correct label, evaluation is less straightforward. We will discuss the distinction even though the applied models in the first half of this course are supervised.
Self-supervised learning is often treated as a branch of unsupervised learning, although it creates a supervised-style prediction problem from unlabeled data. The training data do not need labels supplied by a human, because the data provide the training signal. In language-model pretraining, parts of the text provide targets for predicting other parts. Next-token prediction is the main example: the preceding text is the input and the next token becomes the target.
Large language models are therefore commonly described as being pretrained through self-supervised learning. They may later undergo supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, reinforcement learning, or other forms of post-training.
Using an LLM to code or label political data is a separate matter. At that point, we are using an already trained generative model to perform a classification task. With examples in the prompt, it may act as a few-shot classifier; without examples, it may act as a zero-shot classifier. The task is classification, but that does not retroactively change how the underlying model was pretrained.
crumbs: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI

title: Prediction, Causation, and the Vocabulary of AI
text:
Generative, reasoning, and agentic systems
Generative models produce new content rather than only assigning a predefined label. Large language models generate text by estimating plausible continuations given the preceding context. Their ability to produce fluent answers comes from large-scale pretraining and later post-training, not from looking up a single stored response.
Reasoning models are language models optimized to perform better on tasks that require multiple inferential steps, often through additional training and more computation at inference time. Some produce visible intermediate text before giving an answer. We should not assume that this text is a literal transcript of an internal reasoning process. It is model output and must be evaluated as such.
Agentic systems place a model inside a process in which it can choose actions, use tools, inspect results, and continue working toward a goal. The model may search, run code, retrieve documents, or call other services. This expands what can be automated. It also makes verification harder: if a system searched, selected, summarized, and coded evidence for us, we must still decide what parts of that process we can defend as researchers.
